title: 2 Chronicles 9:29–31
context: 2 Chronicles 9:29–31 closes Solomon’s reign. The rest of his acts are written in the history of Nathan the prophet, the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and the visions of Iddo the seer. Solomon reigns forty years over all Israel, dies, is buried in David’s city, and Rehoboam reigns in his place. The parallel in 1 Kings 11:41–43 names the book of the acts of Solomon as its source. Chronicles does not narrate Solomon’s later turning away, which 1 Kings 11 records, and it takes up the consequences in the account of Rehoboam and the division of the kingdom (2 Chronicles 10). These notes name the difference without supplying the 1 Kings material here. Both traditions read the closing as a sober reminder that even Solomon’s great reign came to an end, and that God’s purposes continue beyond any single king.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, first and last, aren’t they written in the history of Nathan the prophet, and in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam the son of Nebat?
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Solomon’s acts are written in the records of Nathan the prophet, Ahijah the Shilonite, and Iddo the seer. Arminians see prophetic records as sources for the history, and they note that 1 Kings 11:41 names the book of the acts of Solomon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and name the difference by reference. Both traditions note that these prophetic works are not otherwise known to us, and they avoid claiming more about their contents than the text says.

verses.text: Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel forty years.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon reigns in Jerusalem over all Israel forty years. Arminian readers see a long reign of peace and blessing, and they note that 1 Kings 11:42 gives the same length.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s faithfulness in giving Solomon a long reign. Both traditions note that the phrase all Israel marks the end of the united kingdom, which divides in the next chapter.

verses.text: Solomon slept with his fathers, and he was buried in his father David’s city; and Rehoboam his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon dies, is buried in David’s city, and Rehoboam reigns in his place. Arminians note that Chronicles does not narrate Solomon’s later turning from God, which 1 Kings 11 records, and they see the consequences taken up in 2 Chronicles 10.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and name the difference without supplying the 1 Kings material here. Both traditions read the verse as a reminder that even the greatest king died, and that God’s purposes continue beyond any single ruler.
